passage: Snack-time note, Wednesday. Damini pointed toward the biscuit tin and said something short that I heard as "nana," so I brought a banana. Damini pushed it away, cried, and sat with arms folded, refusing the banana and everything else I offered. The snack was late and Damini stayed hungry. I could not tell what was wanted because nothing clear was said. Next time I will hold up both foods and ask which one. Hemant

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when the banana was offered?
qa.a: Damini was disappointed and angry, because Damini had wanted the biscuit and the banana was the wrong thing.

qa.q: What other approach could work for Damini, and why?
qa.a: Damini could point at the tin and say "biscuit" while walking to Hemant, because clearer words and a shown target make it easier for an adult to get it right.

qa.q: How does Hemant see what went wrong?
qa.a: Hemant heard a short unclear word and guessed, and now sees that holding up both foods and asking is a better plan.

grounding: A toddler who wanted a biscuit is offered a banana, pushes it away and cries, because the goal was fixed on one thing and the request was not clear.

passage: Kalyani stood by the grain bin in their house near Warangal, pointing at the top shelf. "Bi! Bi!" Her grandmother Chandrika, peeling a banana for her, held it out. "Here, bangaram, banana." Kalyani shoved the banana away so hard it fell on the floor. She sat down and cried, still pointing at the shelf where the biscuit tin lived. Chandrika picked up the banana and sighed.

qa.a: She was peeling a banana for Kalyani.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she shoved the banana away?
qa.a: She was angry and upset because she wanted a biscuit, not a banana.

qa.q: What else could Chandrika try next time?
qa.a: She could ask Kalyani to point or show her what she wants before offering something, so the request is clear from the start.

qa.q: How does the moment feel for Chandrika?
qa.a: She is tired and a little disappointed that her offer was refused so sharply, and sighs as she picks it up.

grounding: A toddler set on a biscuit pushes away the banana she is offered and cries, because her goal was fixed and her request unclear.

passage: In the Berlin flat, Siddiq tugged at Olga's sleeve and said, "Cookie." Olga, his nanny, was stirring soup and heard "...ee". She peeled a banana and crouched down. "Banana! Yummy!" Siddiq's face crumpled. He pushed the banana back into her hand and wailed, "Cookie! Cookie!" He stamped once, then sat on the floor sobbing, pointing toward the cupboard where the cookie box stood.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when his face crumpled?
qa.a: He was disappointed and angry that he got a banana instead of the cookie he wanted.

qa.q: What would help Olga understand Siddiq better?
qa.a: Asking him to show her or point before she chooses, since the word got lost while she was cooking.

qa.q: How does the banana look to Siddiq?
qa.a: To Siddiq it is the wrong answer to a clear wish, so it feels like not being understood at all.

grounding: A toddler who wants a cookie is offered a banana, pushes it away and cries because his goal is fixed and his request was not clear.
